For the secondary sources, we don't know who they are. We don't know on what basis the Islamic community is saying on the 16th of August, something was blown up. We have to have something a little bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you are talking about witnesses. Were you able to read statements or summaries of statements, and were you provided with transcripts and when?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: In the very beginning of the cooperation with the Tribunal, I was given summary, summaries of the witnesses' statements, and those are indicated in the report. There were then people I talked to when I was going around. It was not systematic, and I'm very careful when I talk to people, when I go around and get the information. And transcripts were given -- just a few days ago, I was given by the Office of the Prosecution, I was given transcripts from this trial, and I was given additional witness statements that these witnesses had been asked only about destruction of sacral buildings. In the summary, summaries of witnesses' statements that I was given at the very beginning mentions of the damaging of sacral buildings would appear, but this is passing information. This is -- I noticed -- it's a different sort of, different sort of statement. So we have two different types of witness statements. The general statements that they're making about what's happening to them, and then we have just a few days ago I was given a number of witness statements that were targeted specifically on the destruction of buildings, mainly in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I may interrupt, Dr. Kaiser is talking about statements which we submitted according to Rule 92 bis, to be admitted according to Rule 92 bis. So he is talking about these statements which were provided to the expert witness, has been provided to the witness recently. Did you incorporate this new information into your report, or did you prepare supplemental to your report based on this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, I mean, I would not rephrase but add something to your question. Was there a reason that you can give us or explain to us why you needed to compile also a supplement to your report? There must have been, otherwise you wouldn't have. So I would like to know is you needed to compile a supplement, and then also the part of the question that has been put to you by Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's partly because I'm a historian. I have a lot of doubts. I have doubts about summaries of witness statements, people looking at something else, and just sort of remember something. I have doubts about something that is cited in a book without backing, backing it up. I did, on some occasions, say that I thought it was important to have detailed witnesses' statements about the destruction of sacral buildings. It was very, very important. We're not talking about 1992 to 1995; we're talking just about a few months -- well, half a year in 1992, and we are awash in a lot of different materials here. And so, in a certain sense, it was -- I'm not saying I provoked it. I think possibly the investigators also realised that it was necessary to do something like this. Does that answer, Your Honour, your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it answer yours, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it was the reason -- and you prepared the supplement, and with the supplement, do the figures change?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The supplement, I think, does change. It changes especially for Sanski Most. Other municipalities may have some interesting summaries. Sanski Most didn't. But Sanski Most now has a certain number of interesting, really interesting statements, that can be sort of compared to dates which have been given by the Islamic community, and also compared to what photographic materials we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when we go to your chronology of damaging, what can we conclude, or better said, what is your conclusion about the damage and destruction of Islamic sacral buildings in the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: On page 2 of the supplement, there is a table which incorporates all the different witnesses, the witness's testimony that was given, along with the summaries of earlier witnesses' statements. And basically, it basically beefs up what might be considered a hypothesis in the first report, the period of damaging of Islamic sacral properties is between May and August, of intensive damaging, between May and August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, before we proceed, just something that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you. You are aware that there are more municipalities involved in the indictment, in this indictment, than are actually covered by your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I should like you to address this because it's of great importance, as you can imagine, because it seems that the report covers only Bosanski Novi, Donji Vakuf, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and -- six municipalities anyway, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the indictment itself, you have Banja Luka, Bihac, Repak, Bosanska Gradiska, Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Petrovac, Celinac, Donji Vakuf, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, Prijedor, Prnjavor, Sanski Most, Sipovo, and Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree with you. And you will also notice that the list under each of these municipalities is not exhausted because it was prepared before we had Dr. Kaiser's report. We can deal it with this -- we can deal it with the changes in our Rule 98 brief, or we can apply for the amendment of the indictment which would mean to withdraw some of the municipalities which we already have dropped. And for the other municipalities which are not covered by the expert witness, we intend to rely on witness statements of witnesses which already which have testified or which will testify in respect to these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But still, I think it is my duty to ask the expert witness, Dr. Kaiser, whether he is in a position or whether he has information that relates to other municipalities that are not amongst those that you have dropped, whether he has conducted any investigations, whether he has any reports, verbal or otherwise, that he could give us about destruction and damage to religious sacral buildings in the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't carry out an investigation to them. But it amounted to destruction and damaging in the other municipalities is the same for this, the chronologies may be different, but it is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The pattern is there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pattern is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My next question to you, Dr. Kaiser, is at least on the copy that I have, your report, not the supplement one but the original one, does not carry a date. I would like to know the date when it was filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The date is right at the end on the bottom of the supplement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the supplement. Were they filed together?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a report, and there is a supplemental report. I know that there is a date at the bottom of the last page of the supplemental report. But there is no date on the -- on any of the pages of the first report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The main report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to know the date of the report, when it was filed with you, or with the registry or whoever, or when it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, are you able to answer this question before we will manage to find this information in our record?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember when I filed the report. It was months and months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, it does mention "until the summer of 2002," so it must have been after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the summer of 2002, yeah. It was sometime in the fall of last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, we have this information. It was filed on 18 of November, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before this interruption, we were talking about the chronology, and in fact, I am now not sure whether you answered the question. Yes, you answered the question about the year -- your findings about the level or the amount of damage which occurred during -- in the period of the year 1992. The numbers which are either in your report or in the supplement, are they correct, the figures which are in your report? Do you want to change anything on what is stated?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: No, I won't change anything. I point out that on page 2, that these witnesses, we put all the witnesses together, you mentioned -- they mention a total of 28 per cent of the Islamic sacral buildings in the six municipalities. That's the witnesses, 28 per cent of the buildings are covered or touched upon by a statement for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also said that you spoke to people on the spot during your on-site investigation, and that you reviewed other materials. Based on your findings and the figures in your report, what do these figures indicate in respect to damage or destruction?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, 28 per cent of the Islamic sacral properties damaged - we know this; we have people who have seen it happen, know about it - are damaged between May and August, that implies that quite an enterprise of vandalism was going on. Whether that is blowing up minarets, setting fire to roofs of mosques - we're only talking here about Islamic sacral properties, we're not talking about Roman Catholic sacral properties - quite an enterprise is taking place over the summer, that is, targeting of these kinds of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you conclude that this damage was accidental or that there was some pattern in this behaviour?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think it's a pattern. I don't think it's accidental. It is -- in the first report, I said it looks like things you could call the blitzkrieg against sacral buildings in these municipalities. When you look at it in detail, it looks like a rather disorderly sort of thing. It's not the same things happening to the same buildings everywhere. It's something else. It's accumulation of different types of destruction of properties that's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Put the same question to you using a different term, Dr. Kaiser: Would you agree that there was, according to your findings, a systematic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was systematic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Destruction or damaging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Systematic damaging, yes, systematic damaging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from what you saw in the other municipalities, the ones that are not covered in your report, would you think that this would strengthen your statement, your conviction, that there was a systematic wanton destruction of sacral buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would find systematic damaging across municipalities. If you looked at the municipalities one by one, you would find nuances and differences in it. But you would find something looked pretty well like the same systematic pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you be able to state the causes of the damage? You already mentioned that the mining, what other causes you came across during your Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 16424 to 16444. evaluation? And maybe we can use photographs or if Your Honours wish to use other photographs, or we can just talk generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I mean, I am satisfied with what I have seen so far by way of description. I do have certain questions that I would put particularly, for example, to one of the mosques that he referred to, I think it's Demisevci. No, it's not the Demisevci. The one that had a little damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Little damage was Demisevci, it was the mekteb, the building without the minaret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unusable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's not that one. There was -- what was the one, the last one, the one before that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We had Donji Agici, which was in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Celopek in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In Bosanski Novi. Maybe we can place it on the ELMO. Your Honour, was it this building you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Could I see the other one, the Demisevci one, please. No, it's not that one. This is one which is still standing, in a way. It seemed that the roof had collapsed, part of the walls had collapsed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Donji Kamengrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Donji Kamengrad. May I see that, please. That is in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sanski Most, Donji Kamengrad. No, it's not that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a photo we had of the mosque seemingly being rebuilt, and there is a gentleman doing some work there nearby, or picking up stones or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. It's Gornji Jakupovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the one, yeah. And this is which municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is Prijedor. Yes. Now, you say here, or rather, in this report or in this statement that we have here, it seems that the cause of the destruction was mining, as far as the minaret is concerned. And roof, as far as -- firing as far as the roof is concerned. My -- what puzzles me a little bit is that it seems that the minaret has been blown up. I don't see it there. And the roof has collapsed. And still, this is considered to be a repairable mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are repairing it. Yes, they are repairing this building. The building, if you take the roof off it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can repair it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can repair it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if the minaret has been blown up, you can't rebuild it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depends where it goes. In this particular case, we don't have an enormous minaret that weighs a lot. And it has come down a little bit on the corner, you see. We have pictures -- if we show you the mosque in Okrec, we can show you really excellent mining of a minaret which is brought down, and it destroys the building. But the minaret is also somewhat different construction, it's heavier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking the question so that you put me in a better situation to understand why two buildings that are, on the face of it, both look very much damaged, and to me would be a writeoff completely are described either "destroyed" or "repairable." I want to know whether the criteria is actually the visual impression and assessment that is made, or whether the assessment also includes as a criterion the fact that it is being repaired and not rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. Maybe we could put next to this picture the picture taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you take Kamengrad, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- In Donji Kamengrad, for example, because the witness will be able to explain why the walls here are still in such a stage that there is possible reparation, and here it is not possible. But it is up to the expert to -- if you could show the picture below. It is the same building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about words, and we are always talking about words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This one has collapsed. I mean, this you can't repair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a good reaction. Because that's exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You look at it and you know it cannot be repaired. I mean, you would be crazy to try to repair that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, you use repairable, and I say rebuilt. Maybe I'm a little slipshod. The problem with this is you often have to talk about rebuilding. We could show you the example -- I understand that the minaret question is of interest to you. We could show you the mosque in Okrec, and then you could see something where the minaret's come down and you can see the building and you can see why the building is completely destroyed, even though the walls are standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see it, please, Madam Richterova. In the meantime while this building is being found, Judge Janu would like to put a question to you, Dr. Kaiser. Judge Janu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, looking at your curriculum vitae, I can see that you are an historian. When deciding the question what is repairable and what is not repairable, did you consult the expert from construction or statistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have worked in the milieu of architects and engineers. I am not an architect. I am not an engineer. I have an engineer who is an assistant. When I have some doubts, I ask him. I have seen thousands and thousands of damaged buildings, I think. I make mistakes. But we're usually talking about a level of damaging to something which is not so difficult to understand. If you went through the Islamic community fiche for Prijedor, you would see the bottom. There are notations who are clearly an engineer's notations. My own satisfaction was that, in fact, that was the same -- it was the same diagnostic except for one building, I think, and I'm not quite sure -- I don't think -- maybe I'm wrong, but I don't think I'm too far off, and I've often asked something about buildings if I had a question. Okrec, I saw first with my own engineer back in 1996 and 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So there was some sort of verification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not systematically, not systematically, but I did consult when I wasn't sure about something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's why I use repairable, which is a large notion, as well. Okrec. Can I explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, this is a mining that is in 1993. The minaret you can see has been brought down very clearly on the building. On the building. It's not an amateur. Lots and lots of minarets are brought down beside the building in the six municipalities, which shows that the minarets are what they are looking for. In this case, the minaret is brought down to destroy the mosque. If you look in the first picture here, just look at the left-hand corner of this building, you can see the wall just leans out. The front wall is destroyed. If we look at the -- sorry. If we look at this, you can see the walls are all leaning, they are all cracked, they are all moved. It simply has to be dismantled. That's all. The building is destroyed. Sometimes, this is brick. This is, I think, solid brick. This is a little bit tougher than hollow brick. Hollow brick is shattered. But this is, I think, solid brick. Normally you put these back together, but not this one. It has just moved too much, the whole building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it's very different from the mosque that we saw in Gornji Jakupovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It also had a concrete structure, it seems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly it was, but I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either a concrete or a steel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably not steel. We have reinforced concrete in the modern structures, and the kind of armature that holds them up and gathers the walls. But the point there is that it's the minaret that fell. It's a different kind of minaret. It wasn't laid down properly on the building. This minaret was laid exactly where those who destroyed wanted to lay it. They were professionals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see that we have ten more minutes. I would like to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have five more minutes because we agreed to stop at 12.25, and I see that Ms. Korner is already here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And because I would like to use the maps, I think I will use the maps after the lunch break. But I don't expect to spend more than probably 30 minutes. But you know that I am very bad at estimating the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps we can stop here for the time being. Ms. Korner can make her intervention. In the meantime, the usher will escort the witness. We will resume, Dr. Kaiser, at 2.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour has been given a copy of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet, I haven't seen the motion as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can summarise it very quickly. It's a very short motion. It's an objection to us calling tomorrow's witness on the basis that although they were given a box of disclosure on the 14th of May, it wasn't opened until this Monday. That's what the motion says. The box of material was not opened and consulted until Monday, the 26th of May. Now, Your Honour, may I say, I have every sympathy for counsel for the Defence having to return after the break for the reasons that Your Honours know about. But it's right to say that the notification that tomorrow's witness was going to be called tomorrow was given around the 16th of May, if not before. Your Honour, the documents about which Ms. Baruch complained this morning, Your Honour, may I say that the most liberal view of Rule 68 was taken in describing them as such. Because they're not translated, but a language assistant was asked to go through them and give a general gist of what they are. They're all documents which are from either late or middle 1993 or 1994. The first is a newspaper article dated the 14th of July, 1993. And it deals with a newspaper that was edited by the witness -- sorry, it's not a news -- it's an information about this newspaper. I'm sorry, I slightly misquoted that. Which effectively says that the editor shows an anti-Serb bias, which I don't imagine will surprise many people given the description he's going to give. The second is dated the 31st of January, 1994, and is a detailed report about the situation in Tesanj municipality, not Teslic. But is details of the forces that were in that municipality at that date, 31st of January, 1994. There is one mention of tomorrow's witness, which describes him as the president of the war presidency of the Teslic municipality with which he will agree. He says that was the position that he took. The third document is dated the 13th of March, 1994, and is an evaluation of the security situation in Teslic in 1994, and there's a mention of tomorrow's witness as one of the refugees who are in certain police, intelligence and political positions. Now, Your Honour, the witness is here. He's ready to testify tomorrow. The documents in our submission can be read by the language assistant who the Defence have working for them. It was pointed out to me that the language assistant had no knowledge of the Defence, that that may be right. But Your Honour, she can certainly give a summary to the Defence of what is contained within those documents. Your Honour, as I say, a most liberal view must have been taken by Rule 68 by the person who took the decision to disclose them. But, Your Honour, our application, and obviously I would like it to be if possible ruled on now or certainly early this afternoon, is that the witness be allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of these documents that date 1993 and 1994? For example, the third document that you mentioned is an evaluation of the security situation in Teslic in 1994. What's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no idea. Your Honour, they've not been translated. They are not going to be used by us. As I say, somebody felt because of course there has been a great deal about the Muslim resistance or the like of it, that may have fallen into that category, or the like of it, and because of the mention of the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you if you have any information as to how many more documents this box had?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That, I can't, without taking instructions. I don't know what -- I think Ms. Gustin can give me a note of what was in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to know before we can actually -- yes, Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: My understanding from seeing that box brought to our offices is that it was about this high, that it had a cover letter that mentioned Celebici - I'm probably pronouncing that word wrong; I haven't seen it in writing - it did not in the cover letter mention anything about Teslic or indicate that there might be information relevant to Teslic. And may I proceed in response as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. My feeling and my position, our position with regard to that, is that the decision as to whether or not this was Rule 68 material was made not only by experienced prosecutors, by even more experienced lawyers. And my familiarity with prosecutors, Your Honour, tells me that Prosecutors do not make that determination lightly. It is frequently the case that I believe something would be helpful to the Defence, that the Prosecutor does not. It was stated that this material was placed in the box on May 14th. As Your Honours know, we did not arrive in The Hague until the 20th of May. And the box was opened and reviewed and we did not get to those documents, not knowing to look for them, until Monday. So that the dates and the chronology of how this occurred, I think is not relevant. But more than, more than that, Your Honour, specifically with a response to relevancy, how could this be relevant to something before May of 1992, I have sat in this courtroom and again and again heard witnesses say "I later learned with regard to earlier events." Now, when I get a summary from a language assistant who is totally unfamiliar with the Defence and our plan of how to attack this case, they cannot know when certain words are important or a certain concept is important, even if they can generally summarise "well, this was a newspaper article that mentions the next witness." And so I cannot rely on the summary of a language assistant to tell me that this -- for me to conclude or Mr. Ackerman to conclude that this is not of importance, and there were 55 pages of documents. I did, I want Your Honours to know, take the opportunity to review the tiny newspaper article with our language assistant today. In fact, I have my own translation in discussions with her and asking her particular information about words. That was easy. But when I get 55 pages of documents and a book this thick of exhibits to read as well as the witness's statement, and to familiarise myself with the other Teslic witnesses, so I get a big picture of what is going on in Teslic, it becomes impossible to assure myself or Mr. Ackerman that these 55 pages are useless, which is what has been suggested. I asked -- I'm sorry. Just one other thing. I asked Ms. Korner if she could assure me that the witness would not say at any time "I later learned..." And she could not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can't expect Ms. Korner or anyone for that matter including ourselves to tell you: "There will be no questions or answers allowed which state `I learned at a later'".

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I only point that out because so many times what they learned later is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it's important. It may be important or it may not be important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just assist on two matters, first I think Ms. Baruch must have made a mistake on the dates we started trial on the 19th, and they were back on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's irrelevant. Your Honour, as far as the witness is concerned, he left Teslic in May of 1992. The area in which his statement deals is the political background leading to the, if I can put it that way, the beginning of the expulsion events in May. Although I've listed the Teslic binder, that's because I haven't had an opportunity to speak to the witness yet. But it is my belief that there will be documents, the only documents that he will be referred to will be the ones that are prior to May, the end of May 1992, plus there's a report at the end which deals, although written later, deals with the early events. Your Honour, nonetheless, none of this deals with the situation. Whatever he learned later, even if he learned that there was a huge BiH, HVO, HOS presence in Tesanj in 1994, it couldn't conceivably be relevant to the events of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a question, Ms. Korner: How long -- if this witness starts his testimony tomorrow, how long is he expected to be here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, originally we put him down for two days. But when I looked at his statement and looked at the documents, I don't think -- he may just go into the Thursday, but it's unlikely. Of course, he is listed for two days. And so if Ms. Baruch wants further time or Mr. Ackerman wants further time, they will, of course, this afternoon and -- I know Mr. Cunningham is taking this witness, so I imagine Ms. Baruch could take this afternoon plus tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also understand unless I have been given the wrong information, you will have a case manager appointed later on today, Mrs. Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: We have requested a case manager. He is not here. So he will not be available to me tonight or even tomorrow night, I don't believe, because a visa needed to be obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. We should be in a position to hand down an oral decision first thing when we resume at 2.00. And more or less, this is just to give you an idea, this is not the first time this has arisen, there was at least two other occasions in the past when we found ourselves in exactly the same position. And the remedy was "move ahead with the hearing of the testimony and reserve to the Defence the right to have the witness be called back at a later stage for a further cross-examination or for some supplemental cross-examination if necessary."

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I just have one other thing I'd like the Chamber to consider, and that is that a witness's bias and motivation to colour their testimony, just colour their testimony, is frequently established by events that occurred after the specific events about which they testify, but prior to their testimony in Court. And that's another reason why these documents may be of very big importance, which we don't know right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies, and also thanks to the interpreters and the technicians. I did not ask for your indulgence, I'm sorry. We went beyond the time. But I wish to thank you publicly. Thank you. We will resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we proceed with the testimony of Dr. Kaiser, there's the decide the Defence motion to reference was made earlier on. This is an oral decision which the Trial Chamber is giving on the motion of the Defence to delay the testimony of Witness 7.113, which motion was filed yesterday, 26th May, 2003. The Defence seeks that the witness's testimony be delayed until such time as the newly supplied documents have been appropriately translated. The newly supplied documents in question are those to which paragraph 4 of the motion refers; namely, three documents totalling 53 typewritten pages which are in the B/C/S language, and a short description of which Ms. Korner gave earlier on during the sitting. The Defence brings forward the following reasons for the request: Namely, the first reason is that since other matters seemed to have priority, for example, getting the trial restarted and running smoothly, including responses to various Prosecution motions, the box of material was not opened and consulted until Monday, 26 May, 2003. The Trial Chamber notes that the Defence had from the 16th of May until the 26th of May to open this box and consult and check the contents, and it is not satisfied with the explanation given to justify why the box should have remained closed until yesterday. Number two: The other reason which is brought forward by the Defence is that the three documents applied under Rule 68 regarding Witness 7.113 would require 53 hours approximately to have -- to be translated. And in the absence of Marela Jevtovic, there is no one on the Defence staff at this point who can read and translate for counsel the contents of these documents. This objection or this ground for the request of the delay is only partly true and relevant only in insofar as it seems that the Defence did not have at its disposal since the 16th of -- since the 14th of May when these documents were handed officially to it someone who could provide the non-B/C/S-speaking components of the Defence team with a proper translation, or at least information as to the contents. This will be taken into consideration in the latter part of the Trial Chamber's oral decision. A last ground that is brought forward is that these documents may very well heavily impact cross-examination of this witness and may also be useful as exhibits during the testimony of this witness. The supposition is that they cannot be used until translated into the English language. The allegation that they may well heavily impact cross-examination is a supposition which is not at all proven at the moment, an effect that they may be used or useful as exhibits during the testimony of this witness will be covered by the decision which this Trial Chamber is taking. Accordingly, the decision of this Trial Chamber is to proceed, to reject the motion as put and order that the Prosecution proceeds with bringing over Witness 7.113, the testimony of whom will be heard starting from the sitting of tomorrow, but reserves the right for the Defence to ask for the reproduction of Witness 7.113 at a later stage should this become necessary and solely on the basis of any reason arising out of the three documents mentioned earlier. Yes, sorry, Dr. Kaiser, you had to listen to all this. Ms. Richterova can conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, before the lunch break, we were talking about the destruction of Islamic sacral buildings. Now I would like to focus on Catholic buildings. Can you tell us what are your conclusions, what are your findings in respect to Roman Catholic sacral buildings.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: First of all, the number of Roman Catholic sacral buildings in the six municipalities is far smaller, about 127 Islamic sacral buildings, and there were 23 Roman Catholic sacral buildings. That leads us to another question, which is -- another point, is that the Croat population in the six municipalities is a totally different order than the Bosniak, the Muslim population. That's something I think also should be kept in mind. When we look at the damage, say, these three different categories of buildings destroyed, repairable, minor, we find -- excuse me, I'm going to be looking in the text. The degree of unusability which I mentioned for the Islamic buildings was 77 per cent. For the Roman Catholic buildings, it was 61 per cent, which means that the amount of damage is, in fact, a bit less. If we look at the number, the percentages of destroyed, it's not 29 per cent, which is what it was for the Islamic sacral buildings; it's something like 13 per cent. Number of repairable but damaged is 48 per cent. So we have sort of different levels of damage. There are also a higher percentage that escape with no or little damage, 27 per cent. But I think -- trying to understand this phenomena, we have to look municipality by municipality. There are some municipalities in which the level of unusability of Catholic buildings is extremely high, for example, Prijedor, Sanski Most, it's also extremely high. These are municipalities in which there is also a large Croatian population. It's the third ethnic group. We go to municipalities that have no -- very small Croatian population, there are three. Bosanski Novi, Donji Vakuf, Kljuc, you find in two cases, two of these municipalities, there's not really -- the buildings are spared, Donji Vakuf, little church which is sort of on the edge of the town, it's undisturbed. The church, very small church in Bosanski Novi, sort of hidden between buildings, it has a little bit of damaged in the roof which, because it was neglected for ten years, turned into substantial damages. But in fact these places where there's only a small Croatian population, the building that's there is not important. I suppose perhaps because the Croatian population is not important. So what I would say is that to be meaningful, to be meaningful comparison, I think you have to take into consideration such things as the demography of the municipalities. And these are just general -- these are general for the period of 1992 to 1995 because we have very, very few witnesses, very few witnesses, only two, I believe, who say something about Roman Catholic sacral buildings. There are more detailed notations about them in the "Crucified Churches," so there is a chronology which is set up, and this chronology also tends to show a lot of damaging in 1992 in the summer months, but starting later. But starting later. It's comparable when you're comparing comparable municipalities. This is my only remark. It is -- looks less systematic or later, but it's also serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Kaiser, I would like to talk about differences among municipalities. And I would like to use your maps. You provided some maps. They are big, so we managed to do some extracts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I provided the Defence with these maps yesterday, and I am going to provide you, Your Honours, with these extracts right now. As we are going through these maps, I will always give you the map. First would be Kotor Varos. Is it possible to zoom it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and first tell us what exactly you were attempting to accomplish by annotating these maps.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I was trying to make it simpler for myself to understand if there are patterns of events that are taking place according to geography. I think that's really basically the reason. It doesn't necessarily help you to visualise a lot more easily, especially when you have, you know, a lot of colours, and you have certain symbols. But my intention was to try to visualise, to understand what may have been going on a little bit better by putting it on a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I forgot to provide you with the legend for the maps. And again, I provided this legend to the Defence yesterday. So now it will be easier for you to understand what red, green, yellow means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you give us just a brief evaluation of your findings in respect to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, first thing is this is a municipality I didn't talk about a few seconds -- a few minutes ago because this is a municipality that has 13 Islamic sacral buildings, and has 10 Roman Catholic sacral buildings, and has a population of 33 per cent, 33 per cent, and 33 per cent. I think it should be kept in mind. There may be enough to know about the dynamics there to draw any hard and fast conclusions. 69 per cent of the Islamic sacral buildings are unusable. 50 per cent of the Roman Catholic buildings are unusable. 31 per cent of the Islamic sacral buildings are in fact destroyed. No Catholic buildings are in fact destroyed in this municipality. And 40 per cent of the Catholic buildings have minor or no damage. Minor damage on this map, this may help you a little bit, are the red or green, the little houses with the roofs. That's minor damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Maybe -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. But I would like to show some pictures. We can maybe show the picture of the church in Sokoline. It's in Kotor Varos. We are talking to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So if Your Honours would be so kind to in the tables go to Kotor Varos. It is the first... It is on the page 03235216 of your tables. According to your table, this is one of the mosque you marked as repairable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, this is marked R. This is a repairable building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I would also like to show you the Roman Catholic church of the Holy Family in Kotor Varos, which is probably quite remarkable example of damage. Can you make -- did you see, did you visit this location, and can you make a comment on this picture and the way how this building was damaged?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, I visited both of these buildings, the church as well at Sokoline. This is the main church in Kotor Varos, so this is in the city, in the capital. This building had two big towers, both sides of the entrance. And these towers carried on the top of them, each tower, a cross. And the towers were mined, and the crosses come down. But the mining of this particular church, it dates -- seems to date from 1993, August 1993. There is mention of damage made about this in 1992, but it's an attempt to put a fire in it on the 2nd of July, and this is actually mentioned by the extracts of minutes of the crisis committee. So there was an attempt at burning, but... I suppose you're also interested in this because this is also -- this is repairable, in fact, is being repaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Just go back to what you stated, so how would you generally evaluate the level of damage in the municipality of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, the level of damage in this municipality is not as high as in other municipalities. What's very interesting is that there is a pattern of damage that emerges quite frequently which is bad damage in a town. This is particularly when you go after a religious building, a mosque or a church, in the town. Now, in Kotor Varos, and you'll find less bad damage outside. I mean, we can go into perhaps the reasons for that later. But in Kotor Varos, the church survives, damaged, wounded, with very, very symbolic damaging to crosses. The mosque in Kotor Varos, which we don't have a photograph for and which I drove past a whole number of times in the past, was damaged, but it was standing. The town mosque. So this is a bit of an unusual pattern of damage. Kotor Varos sort of behaves as a big village, in the town, there's not a sort of urban part of town of damage that is carried out. But there is something which is is interesting, is that one of the traits of bad damage or what you find very frequently is really bad damage is carried out along the road, you see, along the main lines of communication, or roads that are very close by or the minaret can be seen, the mosque, et cetera, et cetera. And we have a few cases of these, these little greens triangles that you can see are, in fact, not far from the main road, and that is a kind of pattern which one finds elsewhere. But otherwise, we find just kind of a mixture of the buildings that are damaged by mining. One of the differences in this municipality is there actually seems to be artillery damage, shelling damage to buildings. Something that is talked about in other municipalities, but over time, you don't see very much trace of it left. But in Kotor Varos, in, for example, the churches here, Jakotina, Sokoline, the mosque Vecici, there are two mosques there, they have shelling damage, it's possible there is shelling damage as well in the mosque in Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Try to place the mosque in Vecici. Dr. Kaiser, are you talking about the new mosque in Vecici, or --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: New mosque, old mosque, they are both damaged in the same sort of way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we can place on the ELMO the new mosque in Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we are still talking about the Kotor Varos municipality. And we can also show the old mosque. And if you can explain on these photos the signs of artillery attack, as you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: This is the older mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The minaret is knocked down. You can see an impact, in fact, on the minaret between -- and on the stump, halfway down the stump. Right there. That's an impact. But in fact, the minaret has been cut by artillery piece. This is not such a good photo, but this is the main, sort of main structural damage that's visible on it. There are other examples of damage. Perhaps the other -- the other mosque is a little bit more interesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you...

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Right. Because the same thing here is we have the minaret is cut, in fact, by an artillery piece. And on the dome, you will see projectiles here, probably up here as well. And then the broken windows. As I say, this is a bit unusual to see this sort of damage, in fact, in the whole area, in the six municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So one sentence conclusion in respect to Kotor Varos? Can we conclude --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: It's not as bad as some. It's bad enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we conclude what you stated in your report, that in Kotor Varos, not one minaret survived?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there's no problem about that. No minarets in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you maps of Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if I missed the exhibit number of this map. What is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my fault. Totally my fault. It will be P1885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the legend?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The legend is the same for all these maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But are you giving it a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can give it number P1885.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we can see the map of the municipality of Donji Vakuf. And again, please, just a general overview on this municipality.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: First thing is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, sorry, Dr. Kaiser. How long do you expect or do you require for your cross-examination? It's a message to Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: She indicated to me before we broke for the lunch break that she had maybe another 30 minutes, let's assume she finishes at 3.00. I still think I can be done by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect. By 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I will probably need more time. And I was also informed that there is a problem with the witness who was supposed to testify on Friday. And so it is also possible that we could go with this witness until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the agreement was that we would do our best, our level best, to let Mr. Kaiser, Dr. Kaiser, go home. You have another 15 minutes to -- another 30 minutes to finish your direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. I will do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So just a brief overview of Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: In fact, this is the municipality that has kind of the lease level of unusability, 62 per cent for Islamic heritage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please slow down. I know that I have only 30 minutes, but the interpreters have to translate.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: You have 30 minutes, and I have all the time in the world. Donji Vakuf has the lowest level of unusability of buildings, okay. You should keep in mind that this is -- not every building is considered in Donji Vakuf because Donji Vakuf is really on a front line zone, there are positions in Prcac, and that changes everything. I really simply eliminated those mosques because Prcac is a front line zone. And then you get into discussion of military use of buildings, et cetera. Small Croatian population. There are -- there is a clear sort of what I would call -- there's a rural damage pattern in the north, you can't see the north. But these are little buildings up in the hills, little mosques, little mektebs and things which are torched, burnt, and some witnesses for two of these in June, not in July as the Islamic documents are always talking about, but actually say nothing in that for Donji Vakuf, but in June here. If you go towards the town, Donji Vakuf, you also have a kind of what I called mixed pattern of damage where again there's not the urban pattern. The big mosque in the town, bas dzamija, carsiska dzamija, is mined. There are witnesses that talk about the mining of this mosque in the summer, and the damaging of two other mosques in the town. The two other mosques are burned. Roofs are gone. One of them is mined. They are squares on the map because they could have, in fact, survived. They are all pulled down after the war. Little red house, it's a little Catholic church which survives. Then you look around coming up towards Travnik, which is this way, and going towards one of the fronts, you have a mekteb up in Suhodol which survives completely, it's a big house. And then, in fact, Seherdik is just a little bit up the road, and it's a mosque which is totally destroyed, recent, recently built mosque. So the little mekteb is completely missed and the mosque is totally annihilated. You have another country mosque, and a mesdzid which is destroyed, and another mekteb we're not a hundred per cent sure it was inside the Serb lines or inside the Bosniak lines. That has only minor damage. So that's the characterisation for Donji Vakuf, not as dramatic as some other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This will be P1886.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then I will start with the map which shows part of Bosanski Novi. So let's start with this part. And again, please, a brief evaluation of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Here, the -- 69 per cent unusability for the Islamic sacral buildings. So it's middling. But what's very interesting here, here there are two damage patterns that emerge which other observers -- what happened would stress a lot and I stress, too, is an urban pattern of damage. If you look at Bosanski Novi, you'll see the little triangles. These are destroyed. This is Gradska, Vitorja [phoen] mosques in the town for which there are witnesses that talk about the destruction and bulldozed afterwards. There's the little Catholic church which is hidden away in its niche and gets away with minor damage. Then we have a little mosque in Urije which is a Bosniak area of the town which is destroyed but not razed. Then we have other mosques along the road in Prekosanje and Buljuk. Buljuk from the state of the terrain, it's destroyed. Prekosanje was bulldozed terrain that was photographed. I'm not sure it was knocked down after the war. This is something I can't say. Now -- but then, when you get to the Japra Valley --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, I will stop you here because Japra Valley continues on this map. So the map which was used by Dr. Kaiser is P1887. And this map will show us the remaining of the municipality of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you were talking about Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, because in fact there's part of Sanski Most on this. Well, up at the top of the other map, you could see some damaged buildings, but not destroyed buildings. And if you look, you'll see all these little symbols that go along the valley here, all the way down to Budimlic Japra, which is in Sanski Most municipality but in fact seems to -- it's really part of this other pattern of damage. These are all buildings that have lost their -- sorry, up here. Yes. They have lost their roofs for the most part. If they have minarets, the minarets have been mined. These are buildings that I say are repairable. And that is more of a rural damage condition; that is, to treat these mosques in the countryside somewhat differently. They have minarets, then they get treated as badly as anything else. Of course, the other thing is that in the country, there are more stone mosques, old stone mosques as well, which means they have the little minaret roof, and that goes, but then the stone walls are left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And on this map is part of the municipality of Sanski Most. So let's start with this part of Sanski Most, and then I will show you the remaining. So again, how would you characterise the damage in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, every case is a little bit different. Sanski Most has 73 per cent of unusable Islamic buildings, but one has to keep in mind a very large number of mosques being constructed. Something like 23 per cent of the buildings of Islamic sacral buildings were mosques undergoing construction, so therefore 73 per cent unusability is maybe a little misleading because if you looked at the usable buildings, the ones that were in function and how many of them in fact were damaged, you would be up to around 95 per cent damage. Catholic buildings are also 80 per cent unusable. This is a municipality in which there is clearly, there is really a lot of damage. And in both communities, both Muslim communities and the Croat communities. It's a municipality where the balance of the Serb population, the Muslim population is about equal. There is sort, as I say, a rather different pattern of damaging. Nonetheless, there are still the nuances, and this particular map, Lukavica, Modra, Gorice, these are unfinished mosques and mektebs, and as a rule, they dealt with minarets somebody is particularly interested in them. Modra mosque, its building materials were taken. Skucani Vakuf is a mined mosque. There are witnesses for this from 1992 -- one witness. Mosque, minaret is mined. It's a stone mosque. Roof is gone. Probably perhaps destroyed, burned in the mining of it. But these are still in the western part of this municipality. These are buildings that can be put into commission or finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will now show you the remaining part of Sanski Most map. This one, which is on the ELMO, can be marked as P1888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we couldn't make it smaller because then you wouldn't be able to see almost anything. So we have to fight with the maps a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. And I see that it wouldn't have been possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I'll try to point out some sort of meaningful patterns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the map speaks for itself. I don't think we need to go into much detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm allowing you to put these questions because they tend to prove the systematic pattern of destruction of sacral buildings, but please don't forget that we're talking for the purpose of this trial the period April to December of 1992. That's about it. You know, I mean, what happened in 1993 or 1994 or 1995 may or may not have been part of a design which existed in 1991 and in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And I think that Mr. Kaiser clearly stated in his report, and we can see it in the table exactly for which mosques and Catholic churches he was able to find the date and for which we do not approve of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So can we just conclude the Sanski Most municipality. What is the pattern? What kind of causes where we can see, cause of damage we can see in the Sanski Most -- in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, you remember there are -- there's a list of witnesses who have said they have seen the damage in this particular period in Sanski Most municipality. I haven't got the time to go through all of their statements and correlate them with the information given by the Islamic community. The bad pattern -- there are patterns of bad damaging. They're along the main road out of Sanski Most towards Okrec, up here. A number of these are in fact damaged according to witnesses 1992, badly damaged. This is -- this urban zone here, Pobrijezje mosque, destroyed in 1992, according to a witness, and also according to documents emanating from the municipal council about cleaning-up operations. Main mosque in Sanski Most, Hamza Bey mosque, also apparently destroyed in 1992. The Catholic church was destroyed much later, although there's a mistake in my report, destroyed in 1995. I would just point out that is an urban main communications route system of damaging that appears, and in fact most of it in 1992, according to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you have nothing else to add to Sanski Most, we can move to Prijedor. And again, very brief evaluation of the municipality of Prijedor, which is on the top of this map which we were just using.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Prijedor has the most systematic, brutal sort of damaging of sacral buildings of both communities, the Bosniak, the Islamic sacral buildings, and the Roman Catholic buildings. In fact, it goes up to 88 per cent unusability for the Islamic sacral buildings, and up to 80 per cent for the Roman Catholic buildings. And you can go back and look at the population balance where the Muslims are the largest population. I'm just looking for things that try and explain simply why there is more brutality in this than in other municipalities. There is the classic urban pattern of damage. Every single mosque in the town area is destroyed and is bulldozed. And the mosques even in, for example, the Brdo area, here, the same thing happens, these little triangles, these are all demolished. In the eastern countryside, you find other examples of complete destruction. The other one in Garabi, actually, in 1995. Everything is square. Everything is a square symbol, for unusable. The triangle for destroyed. This is the situation in this municipality. There are a number of witnesses, but they are not as many witnesses. And there is less information, in fact, on the actual damaging, the dates of damaging in this municipality than on other ones. There are indications that some bad damaging is done a lot later, for example, in Hambarine. Hambarine, which is here, there are two mosques. There are witnesses for the shelling of the old mosque in Hambarine, and hundred metres up the road there's another mosque, and the minaret is supposedly mined, destroyed, in 1992, and then later on in 1995 or 1996, after the signing of Dayton agreement, then the rest of it is destroyed. So there's that kind of damaging to keep in mind. It makes it harder to date things exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it is really showing just two more mosques which we weren't able to see on this map. So the big one, I would like to mark as P1889. And the small one, we can place it on the ELMO just for a second for the Defence to see what I am referring to, the remaining two mosques from Prijedor, I would like to mark as P1890. And I am done with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I have for you a couple of final questions. And I would like to go to your report on page 12. You concluded that - it is under (g), conclusions, the last sentence in the first paragraph, the middle - "given the concentration of significant damage within a period of a few months across most of the municipalities, we are confronted by a targeted, controlled, and deliberate campaign of devastation, a kind of blitzkrieg against places of worship." Is it still your view that it was targeted, controlled, and deliberate campaign of devastation?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: From the point of view of a cumulative effect, yes. If we went through, for example, any particular municipality in great detail, we went through Sanski Most municipality, we would see it's an extremely messy sort of picture. But all these things are going on, they are all going on concerning the same types of buildings. I mean, as I say, it's a cumulative impact. And the question of masterminding of it, the organising of it, that perhaps is something else. I mean, a bit more mysterious. But you're looking, you know, at the investment of human resources, sometimes military resources, to carry out an enterprise which in fact is not particularly productive in terms of moving people around. I mean, in an obvious kind of way. There seems to be -- there's a great interest in doing this, in investing in it at a time when there's a lot of things going on at the same time. And so in spite of it looking sometimes a bit disorderly, yes, I think there's a will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also concluded that "this specific Blitzkrieg was only one element of the large attack, the decisive factor was the removal of the population and the destruction of its homes..." And it goes on and on.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you make a comment on this.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think that's why it's useful to relate the damage levels to population levels in the municipality, to understand what's going on. As I mentioned, it appears that where the Serbs were 50 per cent or the minority, there was a lot more damage being carried out, in fact, against the sacral places of the Muslims and the Croats than where they were in a really big majority. Bosanski Novi, there's a majority of Serb population, and you see, you know, not so much damaging being done to the mosques, the churches almost ignored. I think you have to put the destruction of sacral buildings in that context to understand it. It's part of it, though. It's part of it. There's messages that are being sent when sacral buildings are being damaged and destroyed. And maybe also those that carry on the destruction are maybe forgetting -- it's worthwhile making this investment because this message is perhaps particularly an effective message to send to a population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what is the message?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, the message -- one part of the message is "we don't respect you, we don't respect your system of belief, we don't respect your culture or psychology." Another one is "we don't want you." Many places, the communities, Islamic communities, the Muslims have put the money together, collected the money to build the mosque. This is not just a financial investment; this is an emotional investment. And if you go and destroy this kind of building, you're sending a message to that population. The destruction -- so that's one thing towards the victims of that destruction. But there's the other message that is sort of towards society, where you find the urban pattern of destruction, which is annihilation, bulldozing a monument, it's like saying, "they weren't there" basically. Or even if you left a cemetery, "well, they were there but you left nothing of value." Rewriting history, you're writing history without the other and this history is written in the cities. You're saying something about civilisation, about the past, and that's to your own people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kaiser. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Mr. Cunningham. Before you start, just in case we don't have time at the end, good news. Next week, this coming week, in other words, we were supposed to work in the afternoon. We are shifting the whole week to the morning. So that should be -- prove to be convenient to everyone. I'm talking of the week 2nd to 6th. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number one. Number two, Mr. Cunningham, may I refer you to part of the proceedings of the 19th when Ms. Korner referred to the binders that relate to Bosanski Novi, Donji Vakuf, and five or so from Prijedor. And she had pointed out that to her knowledge, these had not yet been formally admitted as exhibits as yet, that she was under the impression - she could be wrong, though, although she didn't believe herself to be - that there was no objection forthcoming from the Defence to any of these documents. And we had agreed that you would check and come back, come back to me. Yes, Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think it was me who promised to come back to the Court. And yes, we had not made any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So for the record, and for your attention, Madam Registrar, please, all the exhibits to which Madam Korner made reference during the sitting of the 19th May, these are all formally being admitted as exhibits with the number that was assigned to them in the course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would like to clarify only one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When I said that the report of Dr. Kaiser was filed on 18 November 2002, it is the date of the report. The actual filing was 12th of December. So the report is dated 18 of November, 2002. It was filed on 12th of December, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for the clarification. And the last thing is I found on my desk the response by the Defence to the Prosecutor's Rule 92 bis motions relating to Teslic. And I should like to draw the attention of the Prosecution to Mr. Ackerman's response and come back to us, particularly with regard to whether what stand the Prosecution will be taking with regard to points made in paragraphs 2 of the response. Paragraph 3 does not need any -- call for any comments from the Prosecution. It can be attended to by the Trial Chamber. But we do need to know as soon as possible what the Prosecution's position is; in other words, whether it stands by its position or whether it intends to present the statements of the witnesses mentioned under Rule 93 bis. And then there is another document which is an objection by the Prosecution relating to Teslic municipality. Again, I should like someone from the Prosecution to be here tomorrow morning first thing to deal with this matter so that we can hand down a decision on the admissibility of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, there will be someone who can deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So, Mr. Cunningham, sorry for interrupting you like this. But you may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Absolutely no problem. Your Honour, speaking to the Court but with the interpreters in mind, I would ask them if I go too fast for the B/C/S interpretation, that they tug on my robe and give me some sort of warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, I want to visit about your findings, and prior to your testimony, we were given literally a volume of reports that you had prepared in your capacity, some UNESCO reports, some Council of Europe reports. Most of my questions will be drawn from your 12-page report which is in evidence, which is P1883.1, but I'm also going to ask you, it may become relevant to talk about your report from 15 December 1995 as well as your report from 19 January, 1994. That's going to be towards the end. What I wanted to ask you is in that materials that you have out there, are those reports there with you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I don't have my -- I could have access to them, but I haven't looked at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I'm bringing this up now because as a courtesy to the Tribunal, if we need to show you those documents later on, I would ask for the opportunity to do that, and it is my understanding the procedure is for the Prosecutor to provide those documents. So at this point, I would like to give you notice that I may be questioning about his reports, 15 December, 1995, and of 19 January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have the report dated 19 January, 1994, if it is this one. And the 15 December 1995, are you referring to witness statement or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's a document that he authored that is related to that date. That may well be it. If you could have that available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is available. So Dr. Kaiser can inspect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With that, Your Honour, may I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In talking about your 12-page report, you've told us that basically at the time you issued that report, it was limited to those six municipalities. And I recognise that in preparing this report, you had to come up with some definitions, for example, what is a sacral building, because of the nature of the various religions, you had to make, to a certain extent, I guess, what would be an arbitrary decision that a sacral building would be the usual place of worship for the Islamic or Catholic faith. In your report, let me phrase it this way, you come to us as a historian, and as a historian, I take it a healthy skepticism with the information you are provided in the course of doing this report. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in your very report, you talk about some of the limitations on the information that you received that affected, in effect, that information's credibility and reliability. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: For example, your statement, and I don't have the page number, and I apologise, but there was a commonly heard statement that all the mosques in the Republika Srpska were destroyed. That is something that was heard commonly, correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And obviously, that certainly was not the case, and your investigation bore that out. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But at the same time, and to be fair to you, I think your conclusion at page 4 reiterated today was that somewhere between 80 and 80 per cent of the sacral buildings were either destroyed or significantly damaged. Okay. I want to talk to you about the information that you received in how at times you found this information to be - and I'm going to use the word - unreliable. If there's a better word for it, let me know, and we'll work off that term. And specifically, I'm talking about your report -- I believe it's on page 2 where you talk about one of the difficulties you had is determining the actual number of sacral buildings in the six communities. Correct? And you gave us two or three reasons why the numbers you received originally, information provided to the Tribunal for the -- by the Islamic community was not reliable. And could you tell us why that was.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I made an allusion to it a little bit earlier, it's the organisation of the -- simply the Islamic community. The Christian churches have their own systems of administration and administrative districts. And the Islamic community doesn't have it, it's a myriad of Islamic communities. But this means that the gathering of information is rather chaotic. I think that a lot of the problems simply come from this sort of -- they're not really big problems. There are a number of these places. But the -- how shall I say -- it's not anarchy, it's not the right word. A certain amount of disorganisation and lack of types of normal hierarchal structures such as the Christian churches have make it a little harder to find out. There are things that are missing that are unfortunate. Many, many of the sources don't mention such things as turbe. A turbe is a tomb. And a turbe is not exactly a place of worship but often functions as a shrine. So I discovered reading a witness's statement in Trno Varos or Sehovci, some place like that, that there was a turbe there, and people came to that when there is a dry spell and pray for rain. So it's not a usual place of worship but it's very important in terms of popular devotion. And very often, there was no mention made of these, and there are a lot of them, I think, in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me focus in on your report, page 2, paragraph D(i) where you talk about there -- I think you give at least several reasons why, at least with respect to the numbers of damaged buildings as provided by the Islamic community, how it was not reliable. Are we on the -- do you see what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think so.
