utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think one of the things you talk about is that for example, the lists that they provided, that were provided to you, was often prepared in the perspective of reconstructions, meaning that sites that were no longer of interest were left out.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Or sites that may be you wanted to build something on, you would refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So that was a factor that helped account to the -- account for at times the unreliability of the information relayed to you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I'm not really so sure. I'm sort of saying people don't know, in fact, how many buildings there are. To give you an example, very often you have maybe an old building, which is in the process of being abandoned for a new building, you see, which is in construction, or has been constructed. And then people just simply neglect the existence of the old building. For example, in Prijedor Municipality, the investigators went around with the imam, and he showed them this, showed them that, this has disappeared, so on and so forth. The imam did not take them to see a whole series of buildings I found. Those buildings weren't in Omerdic's list, they were in a narrative provided by a local imam, and that's how I found these particular sites. So this goes back to lack of organisation, lack of communication, rather than fiddling things really at the level of the numbers of buildings, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, you talk about how material provided for the Tribunal more recently in 2001 or later is sometimes unreliable, "inflating the number of destroyed establishments". What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Okay, this is true. I give the example of Kljuc Municipality. Where we happened to have a good document by the local president of the board of the community, it's a good document about the history of this community, the ones that don't exist, the mosques that got destroyed and so on and so forth. And then we have a list of buildings provided by the Islamic community later on, and it has two buildings that the imam has said, "well, this one was destroyed in World War II and this one was destroyed at another time." That is -- I don't know what you want to call it, but that's very unreliable, the least that one can say. And you have to take a very careful look. But at the same time, I should say I didn't say here, is that list also indicates a few other buildings that are -- their existence is corroborated in a transcript. But when I went around and asked people, is such and such, does it exist, nobody had anything to say. So it cuts both ways. You really have to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Just recently you talked about Omerdic's work, and then you referred to Mr. Zukic. Am I pronouncing that word properly. Let me talk about Omerdic's work because in your report you indicate interesting baseline figures are provided by Omerdic. What did you mean by "interesting baseline figures"?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: This is a good place to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But then there are also limitations on this work in your study. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What were those limitations?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I'd have to go back to this. I tend to get rid of things that are inconvenient -- not inconvenient, but no longer relevant. I say quite clearly when he underestimates the number of mosques, mesdzids and mektebs in the municipalities of Prijedor and Sanski Most. In the municipality of Prijedor, he indicates buildings that had disappeared before the war. He indicates ten destroyed mektebs in the municipality of Bosanski Novi in the tables of his books. Doesn't mention any damage to the same mektebs, and these mektebs do not figure in the list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you better do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm quoting from myself on page 2, Omerdic, "he underestimates the numbers of mosques, mesdzids and mektebs in the municipality of Prijedor and Sanski Most. In the Municipality of Prijedor he indicates buildings that had disappeared before the war. Moreover, he notes ten destroyed mektebs in the municipality of Bosanski Novi in the tables of his book" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I read it a third time. Okay. All right. "Moreover, he notes ten destroyed mektebs in the municipality of Bosanski Novi in the tables of his book, but does not describe any damage to any named mektebs in the text, and these buildings do not figure in documents submitted by the Islamic community." And I apologise for my remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well it, provides interesting baseline figures, where to start, beyond that do you find it a reliable work in your position as a historian?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: When we go on to another dimension. This is destroyed, this is totally destroyed, that kind of information. Then I start to have problems with these kinds of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Another author we talked about was Zukic, and I want to talk to you about him, because I believe, and stop me if I'm mischaracterising your earlier testimony, that much like Omerdic's, you found this to be a good starting point, but beyond that, you had some questions with it about its reliability as a historian.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I find it perfectly understandable that people feel passionately about these events. I find it completely normal. Mr. Zukic, I think, feels very passionately about these events, this enormous tragedy which happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I feel that people from the international community, that's why UNESCO is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, are trying to lead the semblance of living together, and I think that living together is important and we should work on it. We have a responsibility. I have followed -- used Mr. Zukic's photographs because they are taken in the fall/winter -- maybe 1996 or 1997. They are very useful because they reproduces buildings that have disappeared or have been changed or something. The information given in the texts, I take with a very large grain of salt, about damaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that is because the passion that you've talked about affects his findings and his representations in that book. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say beyond the pictures, photographs provided in that book, and the assistance those photographs gave you in your investigation that Mr. Zukic's work is of limited value?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think it is of limited value. I'm not saying that there are not things of utility in the text themselves, but I think it is of limited value.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to get back to something that you talked about earlier, and that is you talked about how at times, materials provided to you by what I'll call the local Islamic community, some were good, and at other times, some were bad. At times, you found them to be helpful; and other times, I think you kind of just brushed them off, and that's my term, and I don't mean any disrespect towards you when I bring that up. How can you tell -- it seemed to me that the value of the material provided was a function of the particular Islamic -- local Islamic community. Right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: It's a function of the particular community, and I think function of the time that the documents are, in fact, drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How could you as a historian -- let's talk about the particular community. How could you as a historian determine whether it was good or bad? Was that determined on an ad hoc basis based on the particular community? Does that question make any sense?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: When you see something is described in a document, and its condition is it's mined and burned and you actually go and see in fact it is mined and burned, that's a good start. When the document usually says completely destroyed, that's another consideration, but the document has actually made an observant remark about something -- maybe I didn't explain myself completely clearly. But documents that are established for another purpose such as convincing the -- a donor or something like that or what are we going to build, the documents from the Islamic community Prijedor are really very, very targeted, and in some ways -- these are the best ones, they are targeted at the question of "are we going to do this building or not?" So you get fairly realistic comments about the building, which again can be confirmed by what I see on the ground. That does, in fact, correspond to the condition. Now, when you're talking about something like dates, that's still somewhat different. If you feel the general configuration of the document is it's not fiddling, it's not telling lies, it's not drawn up for some other function, then the other information that pops up in it is interesting because that's not part of, particularly, the strategy. This is not so important information to the people drawing up the document. If people drawing up a document, because they want to say something happened here than there, that time, it's a different document, and this is what I felt with notably two of these series from Sanski Most and from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you said. It was often a function of the particular community and the timing. What did you mean by the timing? Is it if it's issued in 1993 during conflict or -- does that affect it, or is it closer to the trial it becomes more reliable? What generally speaking are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: These documents that I'm talking about, I think they're about 1997. Documents that are 1999, 2000, 2001 are closer to this trial. And as they get closer to the trial, then the questions that you and His Honour sort of asked become questions you have to think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Documents prepared in anticipation of a trial are less reliable. Is that what I'm hearing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things -- one of the documents - and I believe it was from Sanski Most - that was the documents that talked about, dealt with trying to convince a donor for money, you found those documents to be -- to have a special indicia of reliability. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think they're -- I'm not saying they're a hundred per cent reliable. I think they are very useful documents to look at closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It brings me back to something that His Honour asked you, and that was about, you know, insurance claims, overinflating insurance claims. How can -- and you know, certainly, I mean no disrespect when I ask this, but if -- it seems to me that if someone is looking for money, that sometimes they paint the picture a whole lot worse than it actually is. And can you see how that could happen? We're going to talk --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's fine. I understand perfectly well. I understand your question. If you go back to sort of the answer I gave to an earlier question, it was if a document said "this is burned and mined" that was good for me. If it said it was a hundred per cent destroyed and it wasn't a hundred per cent destroyed, I ignored that part of it. Any document in Bosnia that has a number on it after the war is inflated. And anything that has six 0s behind it is going to be inflated. It just goes that way. Yes, in this case, a community is trying to fool somebody else. It's not worried about Dr. Kaiser, and it's not worried about the Tribunal. He's worried about the donor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree with me in trying to fool that donor, he could make -- the author of that document could try to make things look a lot worse than it actually was, figuring, we'll ask for a hundred thousand deutschmarks and hopefully we'll get the 40.000 that we need. See could that be a consideration, I guess is the fair way to ask it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Definitely it could be a consideration, but it's of no interest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I know that. But don't you think that that could affect the reliability of the documents?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Definitely. Yes, these are all documents that had to be handled with enormous care. Even the ones that I think that are very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If I've gone over this material, I apologise, but I want to cite you to a passage you have in your report that talks about "partisan works that mix serious information with propaganda, and at times it is difficult to separate the two." And I apologise to you, I can't cite you to the page and paragraph of, that but does that sound like a paragraph you wrote?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I definitely wrote that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tell us what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I'm concerned by all the documents that I receive from religious communities after the war. I'm concerned by them. They mix things. Even a good document is mixing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is that because of the passion that you've talked about with respect to Mr. Zukic, often finds it's way into those documents?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: It's passion, sometimes it's not just passion. In fact, it's something else. It's a feeling, it's the kind of wound that has been put into people because of what they have seen, and maybe that's passion. It's a little different from document to document. It's passion; it's wounds, trying to convince an audience of something, all sorts of elements to this mixture of propaganda and truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to go to the very -- I found this next passage I want to talk to you about. It's the very last paragraph on paragraph 3, in the portion of the very next sentence where you talk about how the local literature is vague and exaggerated, and it continues into the next sentence that -- let me just go ahead and limit it to the vague and exaggerated local literature. Is that again another manifestation of what we talked about earlier about the overexaggeration that you see in these documents?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. If we can also go -- I'm going to take you to paragraph 6F on page 6 of your report, and I don't mean to be -- I take it back. It's paragraph F on page 6. I apologise for that. And I don't mean to be plowing old ground, but at the very last sentence in that very first paragraph under paragraph F, you talk about the ICTY and documents provided to the ICTY. That is, again, a reaffirmation of what we talked about earlier, about the question of documents prepared in anticipation of litigation or the trial. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. As a historian, you can rely on your secondary sources, but it's also a wonderful thing to go out into the field and do your own investigation. And you had the opportunity to do that, and I want to talk to you about that. In paragraph F, you make this statement, and talking about "my field trips were useful in discerning the condition of the site and charting the overall tendency of treatment to the sacral buildings but did not provide many clues --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please read slowly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely. I apologise. Let me take it from the start. I'm at the very first sentence under paragraph F.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: "My field trips were useful in discerning the condition of a site and in charting the overall tendency of treatment to sacral buildings, but they did not provide many clues on the chronology of the destruction and damaging of these buildings during the war." Tell us what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think it's self-explanatory. I mean, there's no date, there's no date on a ruin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: It's fairly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about something that I'll call "rules of engagement" and I think in some of your other reports, you might have talked about -- let's see if I can find it. And of course, I can't. But let me -- by rules of engagement, it could be rules that the command, military command, lays down about how to engage and where to engage and under what conditions to engage the enemy. And do you understand basically what I'm talking about there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I'm talking about your report and your personal observations. Can your -- can you discern between damage caused by what I'll call - and excuse the phrase - legitimate combat occasioned by, let's say, artillery damage caused by an effort to weed out combatants inside a sacral building as opposed to artillery damage just for the sake of blowing something up? Can your reports discern that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The observation of a building does not permit you, and my activity is for the most part linked to the observation of conditions. I cannot decide if something has been hit by artillery, if it was justified or if it wasn't justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that's obvious, and I'm just asking these questions for the record, and I believe you can understand and respect that. You've collected secondary source histories. You've done your own interviews where it was appropriate and where you had the opportunity to do it at the scene. And I know the answer to this, but your report likewise cannot discern whether the destroyed buildings were ever used in a military context by any combatants. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: This is really difficult. I cannot say if something was used. As you get farther away from the war, you get further away from that possibility. Earlier, in the war itself, after the war, there are often traces. There are bullet cases, there is this, there is that. There are soldiers' clothes, there's all sorts of different things. Seven years after a war, it's very, very difficult from the observation of the particular scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With respect, I'm going to talk to you briefly about minarets, and I want to apologise for my ignorance in the area of minarets. Are those much like a church tower, bell tower, are those accessible at all?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: No. They are very accessible. I can feel your question coming. They are very, very accessible, but they're very different from a belfry, a church tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What I'm getting at, can an individual make its way up to the minaret?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Traditionally, I don't know what the person is usually called in Islam, but someone goes up the minaret and sings songs from it, and then areas, say in Egypt, sometimes, you have a tape recorder instead of an individual up there. But you certainly can go up there. Or a record player.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With respect to the urban mosque, did you find - and I'm going to ask for a general conclusion if you can draw this conclusion - were the mosques ever generally speaking at a crossroad, at an intersection in the roadway or...?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I just wouldn't like to generalise. Some are on corners, and some aren't on corners.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's a fair answer, and I respect that. Now, one of the things you've talked about and made reference to both in your reports and in your testimony today was the mining of minarets and the mining of mosques. And I know from prior testimony, prior transcripts that you've provided that have been provided to this Court, that you've testified that in some circumstances, and I'm sure that there are some within the area of your study here, that the minings, the destruction of the minarets was caused by explosives set by someone who had training in the area of explosives. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Much as a historian, you cannot determine what occasion, for example, the artillery destruction of the sacral building I talked about earlier, I would assume that as a historian, you cannot differentiate between who was the person who set the explosive that destroyed the minaret and caused damage to the mosque, you can't tell us whether it was VGS, a paramilitary, or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The only thing I would say is that one would expect that military authorities would do a good job, their engineering troops would do a good job. The one -- we don't have this in the witnesses' statements. But in one of the first trips when I went to Kljuc, I talked to a woman who lived near the mosque and described in rather great detail the procedure of what she considered to be the army to come, lay the charges on the corners of the mosques, to come around to all the houses to evacuate the houses. And this is what I would call very, very professional behaviour. Okay, you're blowing up the mosque but you're making certain nobody gets hurt. Because the mosque is blown up in a controlled explosion with four massive, five possibly charges, and the building comes down at once. And so that's a professional job. Civilians walking around with explosives, they're not going to do that. With more information, one can discern, to a certain degree, who has done what.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think this was -- Ms. Richterova, I'm going to talk about the statement of 15 December 1995 with you want to provide that with the Court's permission and the usher's assistance. I think in there there's a passage, and I apologise that I couldn't put you to the correct page. "In the war, deliberate damage can be imputed to military forces on all sides. It can probably be imputed to civil police and civilians as well." Does that sound like thing that you found --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I found the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That is you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Seven years later, I'm assuming that that position has not changed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: But one learns more over the seven years after the war. Yes, definitely, my position on that would not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about a statement that you made in your 19 January, 1994 report. And I have a surprise for you because I can direct you to the paragraph. The paragraph is 64, and I hope your search bears me out.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I've found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Here, you're talking about what you have called the double dynamic of reprisal and cultural cleansing, and there is a passage that reads something like this, and I will try my best to go slow. "These acts of vandalism are perpetuated by representatives of authority, soldiers and military, and probably civilian police. It can be posited that they are sometimes deliberately ordered by local authorities, but that many of them are spontaneous." Did I get the pass sage right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: To be fair, you're speaking in terms of the BH army and the HZ side, right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I look at the context of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to place it in that context.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the context of -- yes, I think so. Excuse me, if I just can have two seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just take your time.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, it starts on in a general thing and then goes towards HVO and BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Can this same statement be applied to the VGS, the spontaneity of action?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: You notice that spontaneity is also in quotation marks in my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I know that many times it's hard to find the correct word.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I have thought about this a lot over the years, and I think it's very difficult to answer that. There are some spontaneous acts that are of vandalism. For example, the villagers come from a village, and they go to a mosque, and they take this and they take that. I think that's spontaneous, and I wouldn't immediately say that they have to impute that to the mayor or the police chief or whoever. The question, is it -- when people are in uniforms, what degree are they spontaneous? We're saying these are types of actions, types of perpetration, but at the same time, we don't have any clear idea of saying what percentage of the acts are spontaneous and how many are this. But there are some spontaneous acts. They are not so spontaneous when they involve, let's say, a complicated operation of destruction. Right? For example, the one I described. That's different. But then there's a whole gradation of possibilities, and you may have somebody at the other chain who has a pal who has access to explosives to the local mine and says "oh, let's go ask try and do this." And that can be spontaneous. That can happen. We're looking at a lot of acts here which are more organised, more successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: As one of the - and I'm going to change topics on you a little bit, and I want to talk to you about the statements, witness statements, that were provided to you where the sole focus was on damage and destruction to the sacral buildings. Those documents were provided relatively late in the procedure. We'll say, what, within the last year or so, something like that. Let's just say relatively recently.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The summaries of statements were provided a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The other statements that you mentioned were provided a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You've talked -- you've told us how the statements prepared in anticipation of litigation could be unreliable. And yet, we have here statements that are provided to you focussing on the question of destruction; and yet, from a historian standpoint, you find these reliable. How can you differentiate between the two, distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: You'll see in the supplement that I have a table called convergencies which immediately you will understand that there's always a residue somewhere of a little bit of concern. So in the convergency, I try to put this beside dates that would be given by documents. That's one thing. Sometimes there are a couple of witnesses or it does correspond to something else in a summary made earlier. The -- in a few cases, it's also linked up because what we didn't talk about is there are a number of documents that emanated from Serbian authorities, police authorities, and civil authorities that corroborated the witness's statement. I mean, I feel even more comfortable when I encounter that kind of document. It would be far better to have all the documents that come from the authorities in whose name the destruction was carried out than have any witnesses from the other side. I would be much happier to have those documents, in fact. But we have very few of them. The original purpose to establish convergencies in the first report and in this report is to come closer to the truth, to find that there are types of information that corroborate other types of information. You're asking me an existential question to a certain degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I thought all historians could answer those types of questions?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I can't answer an existential question. Each statement has to be taken for what it is, felt for what it is. Some of them seem to be rather weaker than others. But they are not absolute, and I really many happy to put them in a convergency. It's up to the Court to decide what the sense of that convergency is, concerning the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I understand. And again, I'm asking you now kind of questions -- I'm asking you questions in isolation based on some things you said this afternoon. And one of the things you talked about was the church at Kotor Varos, the Catholic church, and I believe it was the one with the twin steeples, and you talked about the destruction in there. And I think you talked about how one of the documents that you used as -- to assist you as an historian with respect to this was something from the Crisis Staff. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was that the municipal Crisis Staff document?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: I think it's a municipal crisis... No, that figures as a note on one of my tables.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have this document with me, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I have no objection if she wishes to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has it not been tendered as yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It has not been tendered because this is a document from the Kotor Varos municipality, and this municipality is still in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we may just have a look at it now and it will be tendered at a later stage, together with the other Kotor Varos documents, not to create a confusion. Unless it has a number already which we will keep later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This has a disclosure number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's not an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It doesn't have an exhibit number yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll just make use of it now, for the record. But it will be tendered together with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My sole purpose in asking him to look at this document was to confirm that it was not the regional Crisis Staff but rather a municipal Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to refer, Dr. Kaiser, please, before you answer the question you just point out that you are looking at a document with the ERN number that you have on the top left corner of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a number on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it's on the right-hand side, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I have 3.213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have this number. That's pages. Then I have 01909955 in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's just for the record. Now proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that is from the municipality Crisis Staff, Kotor Varos municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: This translation does not -- it just says "Crisis Staff." I am really not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Signed Nedjeljko Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Again, moving to a slightly different topic, the maps that you presented to this Court, the various maps that you prepared that have come in as exhibits, do those maps include sacral buildings that were damaged in 1993 or simply those damaged in 1992 based on your investigation?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: It's all the buildings. That's the condition of all the buildings damaged throughout the period 1992-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Final area that I want to talk to you about is in your report, in your testimony, you've talked about the differences between a rural pattern of destruction and an urban pattern of destruction. And I believe you showed us a mosque that fell in the context of the urban pattern of destruction. When you found, and do you remember which mosque I'm talking about? I believe we looked at a picture of it.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Kevljani, I think, the first mosque I think we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would you find that when you saw this urban pattern of destruction, would you find that the damage to the mosque would be consistent with the buildings, say, within a one-block radius of it, or how would you...?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: Well, usually the target is a specific target. Going after a given building, you want that building. And usually certain amount of care is taken to minimise damage around. This is usually the case. The -- if a house has been pulled down because something was burned or mined, I'm not certain that I will know necessarily about it. There are a lot of photographs in the reports, and they very, very often show buildings that are very close by, and there -- very, very often, if they were damaged it's because the windows blew in. The tiles were blown off the roof by the detonation. But you can usually get the sense that destruction is really for that building, and it's not an intention to destroy everything else around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And that's generally speaking, your conclusion. But based on what you saw on your field trips - and I realise it's after the fact and there are limitations because the passage of time and other events beyond your control - but did you ever find the situation where the damage to the mosque would be consistent with the damages to the buildings nearby?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: You're talking about the town pattern now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: The town pattern, now. I think basically, from what I've seen, no, it's a fairly consistent pattern. The buildings in that area around are usually not damaged, but I haven't photographed consistently or looked at all the buildings around, but that's the sense that I have in the towns. In a rural area, you might find something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And your report speaks to that, and your findings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a moment to confer with Ms. Baruch, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, as a historian, I would assume that the more documents that you have, the more sources that you have that can lead you in your investigation, the better. I think that's a given. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you've talked about how at least with respect to the review of the Crisis Staff that you just talked about, you found that document to be helpful in reaching your conclusions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: These are particularly helpful sorts of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If there was, for example, an official document that directed individuals to not destroy mosques or other religious sites, likewise, would that document be important in your investigation, in your findings?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That would be extremely interesting to have. It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember if any documents like that were ever provided to you in the course of your studies?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: In fact, there are very, very few documents that emanate from the local Serbian authorities, in fact. So there is not -- there's not one like the one you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Again, may I have again have one final conference with Ms. Baruch, and then I believe I'm close to finishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You're finding out what a lawyer's last question is. All of the documents that you have based your findings on were either documents that were provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor or the Tribunal, or were documents that you collected in the course of your investigations in this area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe that's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Mrs. Richterova, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I do not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. May I ask you a question to clarify this. This morning amongst the confusion and the documents that we had, I was given four sheets of paper. The first two I can place, they being the first one as being a translation from B/C/S of what became then P1884.2. Together with it, however, there were another two sheets of paper, one in B/C/S, and the other one is a translation of it, a document which allegedly is signed by Mr. Semir Hazic with ERN number 03078845 for the English text. And 01149434 for the B/C/S text. Was that tendered or do you intend to tender that as an exhibit? And if yes, what number are you going to give it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm going to give you the explanation. When I was copying these documents, I included by mistake these B/C/S versions. They, of course, are already part of the documents which we tendered into evidence. I think it was Sanski Most, if I am not wrong. And these translations were just for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But these last two pages, particularly the English one, in which of the other documents that were tendered this morning do I find it? It is definitely Sanski Most, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If it is Sanski Most, then it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems to be Islamic community in BH...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You will find it under P1884.2, and the translation is 03078345. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: 8845, I apologise. So it is really a translation of Document 01149434, which part of 1884.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, I've found it. All right. It's the fourth page in P1884.2. The first two refer to page 1; the last two refer to page 4. Yes, Dr. Kaiser, we tried to keep our commitment with you and bring your testimony to an end. I have no questions, unless Judge Janu has any questions to you, all that remains for me to do is to thank you for having come over once more to give testimony before this Tribunal. It's very much appreciated, also for the objective way in which you have carried out your investigations and prepared your report and your testimony here. You will be attended to allow you to return to your country of residence. And on behalf of the Tribunal, we wish you a safe journey. So tomorrow, we start with 7.113, I think, or something like that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I did not misread you earlier on, you were sort of a harbinger of bad news, what's the problem for Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The witness is invalid, and he is very ill. And we still do not have the doctor's approval to call this witness, so we are trying to find a way to videolink his testimony and hopefully we will know tomorrow morning whether he is able to come; and if he is not able to come, whether the videolink is a possibility, how to obtain the testimony from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is that you must put us in a position where we know if on Friday whether we are working or not working -- whether we are sitting or not sitting. Whether we are sitting or not. The Defence ought to know because they need to prepare for this witness if we are moving ahead or prepare for some other witness, or we are not sitting on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is not possible to bring another witness at such a short notice because this witness was convinced, he was convinced that he would be able to arrive. But the doctor's almost last word is "I do not recommend the journey to The Hague." So we are still -- we still do not know whether the witness would come or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kaiser, please, you may leave. Thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I want is for someone from the Prosecution to put us in the picture tomorrow so that we know whether they need to start preparing for this witness for Friday, irrespective of whether it's a videolink or not. If nothing is going to happen, they don't need to start preparing for that witness; they can start preparing for someone else, someone who will come over next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And the Defence and you will be informed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. That's fair enough. All right. And we will be the last to know presumably. The case stands adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Tomorrow, I take it we are sitting only normal hours, until quarter to 2.00. Thank you.
